sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content:
September 2026 delivered a bifurcated global equity tape, with the technology-heavy Nasdaq Composite posting a sixth consecutive monthly gain while value-oriented and dividend-sensitive benchmarks surrendered meaningful ground as US Treasury yields surged to multi-year highs. The Federal Reserve's first rate hike since 2023 — delivered on September 16 — injected fresh rate-sensitivity risk into the market, while the US-Iran conflict's ongoing disruption of Persian Gulf energy flows sent Brent crude intra-month above **$107/bbl**, amplifying inflationary fears before a partial crude reversal by month-end.

The primary divergence was stark across geographies and styles: US mega-cap technology proved resilient — supported by the compounding AI investment cycle — while European indices eked out marginal gains on energy-sector exposure, and APAC markets split along geopolitical lines. China's Shanghai Composite declined **-3.62%** and Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell an estimated **-5.7%** as oil-import costs surged and the stronger dollar tightened EM financial conditions, whereas Japan's Nikkei 225 held well-supported on the Bank of Japan's constructively interpreted rate hike and continued semiconductor sector strength.

sections.title: Your Must-Know Market Themes
sections.content: Four key themes that shaped markets this month:
themes: Iran War Escalation Drives Brent Above $100 -- The US-Iran conflict entered a new phase of intensity in September, with sustained strikes on Persian Gulf energy infrastructure and renewed threats to close the Strait of Hormuz — through which roughly one-fifth of global oil historically transited — pushing Brent crude to an intra-month high of **$107.46/bbl** on September 15. The IEA characterised the disruption as the largest geopolitical oil supply shock in history, triggering emergency strategic reserve releases from member nations and accelerating global investment in alternative supply routes and LNG infrastructure. By month-end, Brent partially reversed to **$98.03/bbl** as diplomatic signals of a partial supply corridor agreement tempered the panic, still posting a monthly gain of **+8%** from the August close of **$90.80/bbl**. The oil spike cascaded into broader inflationary expectations, complicating the policy calculus for every major central bank simultaneously navigating the dual mandate of price stability and growth support.

Federal Reserve Restarts Rate Hike Cycle -- In a unanimous 12-0 vote on September 16, the FOMC raised the federal funds target range by **25 basis points** to **3.75%–4.00%** — the first rate increase since 2023, following five consecutive hold decisions. Fed Chair Warsh cited the "resilience of the US economy," with full employment maintained and headline inflation above the **2%** target, in part due to energy-driven price pressure amplified by the Iran conflict. The updated dot plot was decidedly hawkish: 16 of 18 officials anticipated at least one additional hike before year-end, with the median projection placing the terminal rate at **4.1%** by end-2026 — setting the stage for continued front-end yield pressure in Q4. Markets reacted swiftly: the US 10-year yield surged **+56 basis points** over September to close at **5.29%**, and rate-sensitive equity sectors — real estate, utilities, consumer staples — bore the brunt of the subsequent de-rating.

AI Mega-Cap Bifurcation: Nasdaq Leads as Dow Trails -- September saw the widest monthly divergence between the Nasdaq Composite and the Dow Jones Industrial Average of the current cycle, with the Nasdaq advancing **+1.9%** to close at **26,861** while the Dow shed **-4.3%** to **50,908** — a spread of more than **600 basis points** that crystallised the structural rotation underway within US equities. AI-exposed mega-caps — Nvidia, Alphabet, Meta, and Microsoft — held firm or posted gains as the AI infrastructure build-out superseded rate-driven valuation headwinds, buoyed by strong data centre order flows and undiminished corporate AI adoption spend; forward earnings estimates for the technology sector continued to grind higher, providing fundamental justification for the multiple resilience. By contrast, the Dow's value-cyclical composition — weighted toward financial services, industrials, consumer brands, and healthcare — bore disproportionate exposure to the rising rate environment and oil-driven input cost inflation. The S&P 500 split the difference, declining only **-0.4%** to **7,652**, as the index's meaningful technology weighting provided partial insulation against the broader market selloff.

Treasury Yield Surge to Multi-Year Highs -- The US Treasury market experienced its most significant single-month yield sell-off of the current tightening cycle in September, with the benchmark 10-year yield rising from **4.73%** at end-August to **5.29%** by month-end — the highest level since November 2023. The move reflected the compounding of three concurrent forces: the Fed's surprise-hawkish rate hike, the inflationary signal from oil crossing **$100/bbl** intra-month, and growing investor concern over US fiscal sustainability requiring structurally higher term premia. The 2-year Treasury yield closed September at **4.88%**, producing a **41 basis point** positively sloped 2s10s curve — a tentative steepening suggesting markets are beginning to price higher long-run neutral rates rather than near-term easing alone. The global rate repricing was synchronised: Gilts and Bunds rose in sympathy, peripheral eurozone spreads widened, and duration assets globally posted their largest single-month drawdown of 2026 as equity and bond declines coincided — the classic stagflationary feedback loop beginning to assert itself in asset prices.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
US equity markets delivered a net negative month for the broad tape, with the S&P 500 declining **-0.4%** to close at **7,652** and the Dow Jones Industrial Average shedding **-4.3%** to **50,908** — the worst monthly Dow performance of 2026. The Federal Reserve's September 16 rate hike — unanimous and accompanied by a hawkish dot plot projecting the fed funds rate reaching **4.1%** by year-end — acted as the primary catalyst for the rotation out of rate-sensitive sectors, as investors rapidly re-priced the interest-rate outlook following five consecutive hold decisions.

The Nasdaq Composite was the notable outlier, gaining **+1.9%** to close at **26,861**, as AI-exposed megacap technology names proved largely immune to the rate headwind. The fundamental justification was consistent: robust AI infrastructure spend, rising enterprise software adoption rates, and forward earnings estimates that continued to move higher for the largest technology companies despite the macro headwinds. Nvidia remained a focal point, with continued data centre revenue strength underpinning the bullish case even as the broader market de-rated on duration concerns.

Sector dispersion was extreme: technology and communication services posted gains while real estate, utilities, and financials — each adversely affected by higher yields or compressed net interest margins — logged sharp losses. Consumer discretionary also underperformed as higher oil prices translated into elevated fuel costs pressuring household spending capacity. September's tape reinforced the dominant 2026 equity cycle theme: AI megacap quality provides a resilient index-level floor, but breadth beneath the surface remains dangerously narrow, and the next earnings season will test whether AI-driven profit growth can sustain the divergence.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equity markets ended September with marginal gains across the board, with the FTSE 100 leading continental peers at **+1.30%** for the month, supported by its outsized exposure to energy majors that benefited directly from the **+8%** monthly advance in Brent crude. The DAX finished effectively flat at **+0.13%** — settling near **26,604** — as Germany's industrial and export-oriented composition was caught between the positive effect of dollar strength on euro-denominated earnings and the rising input cost burden of elevated energy prices for manufacturing. The CAC 40 posted a modest **+0.85%** advance.

The European Central Bank held no scheduled meeting in September, but the energy supply shock materially shifted the ECB's near-term rate outlook. Policymakers signalled renewed concern about headline inflation resurgence driven by oil — feeding directly into European consumer energy prices through fuel and heating costs — and the implied probability of an ECB rate hike in Q4 2026 rose meaningfully in OIS markets. European sovereign yields rose in lockstep with US Treasuries, with peripheral spreads — Italian BTPs versus German Bunds in particular — widening modestly as higher rates pressured weaker sovereign credits.

The structural bifurcation within European equities continues to sharpen: FTSE 100 energy and mining heavyweights — BP, Shell, Rio Tinto, Glencore — generated outsized gains, while rate-sensitive continental sectors including property, utilities, and financials faced headwinds from rising sovereign yields. The eurozone macro backdrop deteriorates at the margin: energy import costs are rising again, Chinese demand is softening, and the ECB appears to be shifting from pause back toward potential tightening — a combination that clouds European equity upside heading into year-end.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Japan's Nikkei 225 closed September at **66,753.72**, navigating Silver Week holiday closures in late September and recovering from a mid-month trough near **65,018** in the wake of the Bank of Japan's rate hike to **1.25%** — the highest policy rate since 1995. The BOJ move, widely anticipated following hawkish August forward guidance, was interpreted constructively as a signal of genuine economic and wage growth momentum rather than destabilising tightening, and Japanese equities rallied into month-end led by SoftBank, semiconductor-related names, and export corporates buoyed by the still-elevated yen carry differential. The Nikkei's year-to-date gain stood at **+29%** through September, reflecting the compounding effect of AI-driven tech earnings and accelerating corporate governance reform.

China's equity markets faced material pressure. The Shanghai Composite declined **-3.62%** as the combined headwinds of surging oil import costs, a stronger dollar tightening EM financial conditions, and persistent uncertainty about the property sector recovery weighed on domestic investor sentiment. The Hang Seng Index underperformed even more sharply, falling an estimated **-5.7%** to close near **24,119**, as Hong Kong-listed names — carrying greater sensitivity to global risk sentiment and foreign capital flows than the domestically dominated A-share market — were caught in the crossfire of macro deterioration and renewed US-China technology restriction concerns.

The APAC divergence in September — Japan resilient while Chinese markets declined — reflects fundamentally different macroeconomic trajectories. Japan is experiencing genuine wage-driven inflation that validates BOJ normalisation, while China faces an external terms-of-trade shock from higher oil and a domestic demand environment that remains below pre-pandemic trend. This contrast creates a meaningful intra-regional allocation debate for APAC-focused portfolio managers, and the divergence is likely to persist into Q4 absent a meaningful commodity price reversal or targeted Chinese fiscal stimulus.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
The US Dollar Index (DXY) advanced **+2%** in September to settle near **101.5**, posting its strongest monthly performance since June as two powerful dollar-bullish forces converged simultaneously: the Fed's hawkish pivot delivering its first rate hike since 2023 and safe-haven demand tied to the escalation of the US-Iran conflict. The advance was broad-based across most major currency pairs, with the Japanese yen as the sole meaningful exception.

GBP/USD fell sharply from **1.3600** at month-open to **1.3252** by September 30, a decline of **-2.6%**, as the Bank of England maintained a cautious data-dependent stance that left sterling poorly positioned against a resurgent dollar. EUR/USD declined from **1.1593** at end-August to near **1.136** — a move of roughly **-2%** — reflecting the euro's reduced yield-differential appeal as Fed tightening resumed while the ECB remained on hold through September. USD/JPY, by contrast, fell modestly from **157.4** to around **156.4** as the Bank of Japan's **25bp** rate hike to **1.25%** provided measured yen support, making it the only major currency to strengthen against the dollar during the month.

The FX dynamics of September crystallised a key macro thesis for the remainder of 2026: the dollar's trajectory is no longer a simple function of relative rate differentials but is increasingly shaped by the geopolitical oil shock and its asymmetric impact on current account balances across major economies. Oil-importing blocs — Europe, Japan, South Korea, and China — face structurally weaker currencies unless their central banks respond with matching rate increases, creating a differentiated FX landscape that rewards policy-normalising central banks and penalises those still in pause mode.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
Energy markets were the defining commodity story of September, with the US-Iran conflict triggering the most severe intra-month oil price spike since the conflict's onset in February. Brent crude surged to an intra-month high of **$107.46/bbl** on September 15 amid acute fears of a Strait of Hormuz closure, before partially retreating to **$98.03/bbl** by month-end as emergency IEA strategic reserve releases and signals of a partial supply corridor agreement tempered the extreme risk premium. The monthly gain from the August close of **$90.80/bbl** was **+8%**. WTI crude tracked a similar arc — peaking at **$102.43/bbl** on September 16 before closing the month at **$90.42/bbl** as US shale producers accelerated rig deployments in response to the elevated price signal.

Gold ended September near **$4,399/oz**, a modest **-0.7%** decline from the August close of **$4,431/oz**, as the dollar's **+2%** monthly advance created headwinds for the metal in USD terms. The slight monthly decline masked significant intra-month volatility: gold fell from its August highs as the Fed's hawkish rate hike boosted real yields — the principal opportunity cost of holding non-yielding bullion — before finding renewed safe-haven support from geopolitical escalation that partially offset the rate headwind. Copper traded flat at near **$6.35/lb**, as supply disruptions from Chilean mining operations were broadly offset by demand concerns tied to a stronger dollar and softer Chinese growth data.

The commodity landscape heading into Q4 presents a challenging policy environment: oil structurally above **$90/bbl** introduces persistent headline CPI pressure across the global economy, while gold's resilience near all-time highs signals sustained institutional appetite for macro hedges. The divergence between energy outperformance and base metals consolidation reflects the market's verdict that this commodity cycle is geopolitically driven rather than demand-driven — a distinction with important implications for how central banks interpret and respond to the resulting inflationary signal.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
September 2026 was a watershed month for US Treasuries, with the 10-year yield surging **+56 basis points** from **4.73%** at end-August to **5.29%** at month-end — the highest level since November 2023 and a move that reverberated across global fixed income markets. The primary catalyst was the FOMC's unanimous September 16 rate hike to a target range of **3.75%–4.00%**, accompanied by a dot plot signalling the median official projected the funds rate reaching **4.1%** by end-2026 — implying at least one additional hike in Q4. The 2-year Treasury yield closed at **4.88%**, with the resulting **41 basis point** positively sloped 2s10s curve representing a tentative bear steepening consistent with markets pricing higher long-run neutral rates rather than merely adjusting near-term policy expectations.

The velocity and breadth of the Treasury sell-off reflected three concurrent drivers: the Fed's hawkish policy pivot, the inflationary signal from oil crossing **$100/bbl** intra-month, and growing investor concern over US fiscal sustainability as the deficit widens at a cyclical growth peak — a combination that has reintroduced bond vigilante dynamics for the first time since the 2022–2023 tightening cycle. The term premium embedded in long-dated Treasuries appears to be re-pricing structurally higher, and the distinction between a cyclical rates overshoot and a secular shift in the neutral rate is becoming an increasingly live debate in fixed income strategy.

Globally, developed market government bonds sold off in sympathy with Treasuries: UK Gilt yields rose sharply, German Bund yields tested levels that raised ECB credibility questions, and peripheral eurozone spreads widened as higher global rates pressured weaker sovereign credits. For fixed income investors, September dramatically compressed the expected duration of the current rate plateau, and positions in long-dated bonds suffered their largest single-month mark-to-market losses of 2026 — reinforcing the case for short-duration and barbell positioning over the long end of the curve into year-end.
